transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new community bike share program launched in Manchester, England, this month is already seeing record ridership, with over 15,000 trips taken in the first two weeks of operation. The program, called "MCR Bikes," features 500 bright green bicycles stationed at 60 docking stations across the city center and surrounding neighborhoods, available for rent through a smartphone app. Riders can unlock bikes for just one pound per 30 minutes, or purchase a monthly membership for fifteen pounds that includes unlimited hour-long rides. City transportation officials designed the program to reduce traffic congestion and air pollution while providing an affordable transportation option for residents and visitors. Early data shows that the bikes are being used for both commuting and recreational purposes, with peak usage during morning and evening rush hours and on weekends near parks and shopping districts. Manchester is the latest UK city to launch a major bike share program, following successful initiatives in London, Glasgow, and Bristol. The city has also recently added over 20 kilometers of protected bicycle lanes to support the program and encourage more people to cycle.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: The city of Boston, Massachusetts, is implementing a pioneering program to reduce stormwater flooding by installing green infrastructure in public schoolyards. Over the next two years, the city will transform eight schoolyards by replacing asphalt and concrete with permeable pavements, rain gardens, native trees, and underground water storage systems. These features are designed to absorb heavy rainfall and prevent stormwater from overwhelming the city's aging sewer system, which frequently causes street flooding and sewage overflows during major storms. The "Green Schoolyards" initiative will cost 12 million dollars, funded through a combination of city environmental bonds and federal grants. In addition to flood mitigation, the redesigned schoolyards will provide shaded outdoor learning spaces, new playground equipment, and natural habitats for birds and butterflies. Students at the participating schools will also be involved in maintaining the gardens and learning about environmental science through hands-on activities. City planners say that if the pilot program is successful, they hope to expand green infrastructure to more than 100 additional schools and public parks over the next decade. Climate scientists note that New England has seen a 70 percent increase in heavy rainfall events since 1950, a trend they attribute to climate change.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A new report from the United Nations World Tourism Organization shows that international tourism has almost fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels, with 88 percent of pre-2019 tourist arrivals recorded in the first half of 2025. The recovery has been led by strong growth in Southern Europe and the Middle East, which have already exceeded 2019 arrival numbers by 12 percent and 15 percent respectively. However, Asia and the Pacific region has been slower to recover, reaching only 75 percent of pre-pandemic levels due to varying visa policies and slower reopening in some countries. France remains the most visited country in the world, with Spain, the United States, Turkey, and Italy following closely behind. The UNWTO report notes that tourists are increasingly seeking sustainable travel options and experiences focused on nature and local culture, rather than traditional mass tourism destinations. Spending by international tourists is also expected to reach 1.4 trillion dollars in 2025, supporting millions of jobs in the hospitality and travel sectors worldwide. Experts caution that rising airline fuel costs and economic uncertainty could slow the recovery in the second half of the year, though they remain cautiously optimistic about the industry's overall trajectory.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Jessica): Hi Mark, did you finish the reading for our sociology class today? I found the chapter on social media and relationships really interesting, but I wasn't sure about some of the research findings.

Man (Mark): I did, actually. I thought it was fascinating how the study found that people who use social media heavily actually report feeling more lonely, not more connected. That seems counterintuitive, right? You'd think having all those online friends would make people feel less alone.

Woman: I know, that's what surprised me too. But the researchers said it's because online interactions don't provide the same depth as in-person conversations. When you're just scrolling through photos and reading short posts, you're not getting the emotional support that comes from actually talking with someone face to face. Did you get to the part about comparison culture?

Man: Oh right! The part about how people mainly post their best moments on social media, so when you see everyone else's perfect vacations and achievements, you start feeling like your own life is boring or inadequate by comparison. The study found that increased Instagram use was particularly linked to higher rates of anxiety and depression among teenagers.

Woman: Exactly. But wait, it's not all negative, right? The reading also talked about how social media helps people maintain long-distance relationships. Like, if your family lives far away, being able to see photos and video chat regularly can help you feel connected even when you can't be together.

Man: That's a good point. I think the takeaway is that it's all about how you use it. Passively scrolling for hours seems to be bad for mental health, but actively using it to message friends, plan events, or join groups that share your interests can actually be positive. The research recommended limiting mindless scrolling to 30 minutes a day.

Woman: Thirty minutes a day? That seems impossible for me. I probably spend at least two hours on my phone daily just checking social media. But maybe I should try setting a timer. Our paper is due next week—are you going to focus on the negative effects or the positive ones?

Man: I'm thinking of focusing on the balance, maybe comparing different age groups. The data showed that older adults actually benefit more from social media because it helps them stay connected after retirement, while teenagers are more negatively affected by comparison.

paras: Man (Edward): Good morning, Anna! How was your weekend? I heard you went to that new vintage clothing market in Shoreditch.

Woman: It really is. I used to buy cheap clothes from fast fashion brands all the time, but they'd fall apart after just a few washes, and then I'd throw them away and buy more. It's such a wasteful cycle. Since I started buying vintage and secondhand, I've actually saved money too, because the quality is so much better.

Natural materials like wool, cotton, and linen last much longer than cheap synthetics. Also, don't worry too much about size—vintage sizes run really differently, so you have to try things on.

Also, there are some good apps now where people sell secondhand clothes directly. I've found some great pieces on Depop too. You should come with me to the market next month!

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The concept of "micro-habits" has gained significant attention in psychology and self-help circles in recent years, and for good reason. Micro-habits are tiny, easy-to-perform actions that require minimal motivation to complete—things like reading one page of a book, doing two push-ups, or drinking one glass of water first thing in the morning. The key insight behind micro-habits is that people often fail at habit formation because they set overly ambitious goals that require too much willpower to maintain, especially when starting out. When a habit is so small that it feels almost ridiculous to skip, it becomes much easier to stick with consistently. Over time, these tiny actions compound. Research shows that once you perform a micro-habit consistently for several weeks, you naturally begin to do more without having to force yourself—the person who starts with one push-up often finds themselves doing ten or twenty after a month simply because they're already in the position and it feels good. Micro-habits also leverage the psychological principle of consistency: once you've done something small every day, your brain starts to identify with the behavior, making it easier to continue. For example, if you read just one page every night, you start seeing yourself as "someone who reads," which motivates further reading. Studies on willpower suggest that our daily supply of self-control is limited, so starting with tiny changes that don't drain that willpower is a more sustainable approach than dramatic overhauls. The success rate for people who adopt micro-habits is estimated to be around 80 percent, compared to roughly 30 percent for those who attempt major lifestyle changes all at once.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: The Shetland Islands, located off the northeast coast of Scotland, are home to a unique breed of small ponies that have captured hearts around the world. Shetland ponies stand at most 42 inches tall at the shoulder, making them one of the smallest horse breeds in existence, yet they are known for their incredible strength relative to their size—they can pull up to twice their own body weight, a feat that would be impossible for most full-sized horses. The breed has lived on the Shetland Islands for over 2,000 years, brought there by Bronze Age settlers and later influenced by Norse settlers who arrived in the 9th century. The harsh climate of the islands—characterized by strong winds, cold temperatures, limited vegetation, and rough terrain—shaped the ponies' evolution, giving them their thick double coats, stocky build, sturdy legs, and hardy, sure-footed nature. Historically, Shetland ponies were used by island residents for a variety of tasks including pulling carts, carrying peat for fuel, and plowing small fields. During the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century, thousands of Shetland ponies were brought to mainland Britain to work in coal mines, where their small size allowed them to navigate narrow underground tunnels pulling carts of coal. Today, Shetland ponies are popular around the world as children's riding ponies, show animals, and companion animals. They are also increasingly used in animal-assisted therapy programs, where their gentle temperament and small size make them ideal for working with children and people with disabilities. Every January, Shetland hosts the Up Helly Aa fire festival, where costumed participants include representations of the famous ponies.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: Urban planning trends have shifted dramatically over the past 60 years, particularly regarding how cities approach public spaces and walkability. In the 1950s and 1960s, many cities in North America and Europe designed neighborhoods around the automobile, building wide highways, large parking lots, and sprawling suburbs that required a car for nearly all activities such as shopping, going to school, or visiting friends. Downtown areas declined as people moved to suburbs, and public spaces were often designed to move cars quickly rather than to accommodate people on foot. However, starting in the 1980s and accelerating in recent decades, city planners have begun reversing this approach, recognizing that walkable neighborhoods lead to healthier, more connected, and economically vibrant communities. Modern urban design now emphasizes mixed-use development—where apartments, shops, restaurants, offices, and parks are located close together—along with wide sidewalks, bicycle lanes, public plazas, and accessible public transportation. Research consistently shows that residents of walkable neighborhoods have lower rates of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease because they incorporate physical activity like walking into their daily routines. These neighborhoods also tend to have stronger community ties, as people encounter their neighbors more frequently when they are out walking rather than isolated in cars. Property values in walkable areas have increased significantly over the past 20 years, often by 15 to 30 percent compared to car-dependent suburbs. Cities like Copenhagen, Amsterdam, and Portland, Oregon, have led this transformation, investing heavily in pedestrian infrastructure and reducing car traffic in city centers. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated this trend, as cities temporarily closed streets to cars to create more space for outdoor dining and recreation, and many of these changes have become permanent.
